vignette:
Gerald is a 72-year-old software engineer of Canadian descent, currently living alone in a modest apartment in the Pacific Northwest. He came to the clinic quietly, almost reluctantly, describing his situation in measured technical language - the habit of a man who has spent decades reasoning through problems in code. What he could not reason his way out of was what had happened to him fourteen months earlier, during what was supposed to be a brief consulting trip abroad. Gerald had been detained by local security forces under circumstances that remain legally unresolved. Over the course of several days, he was subjected to systematic physical and psychological torture - confined in a windowless room, deprived of sleep, subjected to threats delivered by men whose faces he could not read but whose expressions he learned to parse for the difference between a warning and an intention. He was eventually released without explanation, flown home, and told by the consulate to be grateful. He arrived back in Seattle in October with bruised ribs and no language for what had happened to him.

In the months that followed, Gerald found that the world had become a place of unreadable danger. He had come to believe, with a quiet and terrible certainty, that people's faces contained information he needed to survive - that the slight tightening around a stranger's eyes, or the way a colleague shifted his weight in a doorway, might be the only warning he would receive before something happened again. At work, seated at his desk in an open-plan office, he spent more time watching the room than reading his code. He catalogued the postures of the men who walked behind him. He could not explain this to his manager, and so he said nothing, but his output slowed and his reviews suffered. This hypervigilance around the faces of others fed directly into a growing conviction that the world was fundamentally unsafe - that the faith he had once placed in institutions, in colleagues, even in the basic predictability of human behaviour, had been naive. He had lost something he could not name but felt as a kind of structural damage, as though a load-bearing wall inside him had been removed.

That sense of threat did not stay at the office. Each evening, returning to his apartment, Gerald found himself checking the locks on his door and the latches on his windows before he could sit down - then checking them again an hour later, and again before bed. He could not fall asleep without this ritual, and even then sleep came reluctantly, because some part of him remained convinced that staying alert was the only thing standing between him and another room with no windows. The threat he perceived in his environment had gradually shaped a set of habits that made his life smaller and more exhausting, and he was aware, in his more lucid moments, that these habits were not making him safer - only more consumed.

What disturbed Gerald most, and what he struggled most to articulate, was the sense that he had become someone he did not recognise. During his detention he had said things - or failed to say things - that he could not square with his understanding of himself as a principled man. He had acted in ways that went against who he believed himself to be, and this knowledge sat in him like a splinter. His attempts to manage this were characterised by constant internal surveillance: he monitored his own thoughts for what he feared might be signs of moral disintegration or psychological unravelling, as though catching a bad thought early enough might prevent some larger collapse. He also tried hard not to think about the trauma at all, suppressing memories with the same disciplined effort he might apply to a difficult debugging problem. And yet the monitoring and suppression together only deepened his conviction that something was fundamentally wrong with him - that a man who had to watch himself this carefully must already be broken. He avoided being alone in enclosed spaces when he could, though the irony of this was not lost on him, given that he lived alone.

Gerald arrived at the clinic after his employer suggested, gently but firmly, that he seek support. He does not expect to be understood. What he is most afraid of is that the clinician will confirm what he already suspects - that the man who came back from that room is not the man who went in.
